questions.prompt: A bacterium has NO cell wall at all, yet still causes disease. How would Penicillin most likely affect it?

options.text: Penicillin would work exceptionally well since there's no wall to protect it
Penicillin would be ineffective, since it targets peptidoglycan cross-linking, which this organism doesn't have
Penicillin always kills bacteria regardless of cell wall status
This organism cannot be affected by any antibiotic at all

questions.explanation: This describes Mycoplasma. Since Penicillin's mechanism depends entirely on peptidoglycan cross-linking, an organism with no cell wall gives it nothing to act on.

questions.prompt: Which structural feature distinguishes a Gram-negative cell from an Acid-Fast cell, even though neither has the extremely thick peptidoglycan layer typical of Gram-positive cells?

options.text: Gram-negative cells have an outer membrane with LPS; Acid-Fast cells have mycolic acid instead, with no outer membrane
Gram-negative cells have mycolic acid; Acid-Fast cells have an outer membrane
Acid-Fast cells have a thicker peptidoglycan layer than Gram-positive cells

questions.explanation: Gram-negative cells are defined by their outer membrane and LPS; Acid-Fast cells lack an outer membrane but add waxy mycolic acid onto a peptidoglycan layer more like Gram-positive cells.

questions.prompt: Which two structures would most directly help a bacterium both attach to a host's cells and resist being physically flushed away, in the early stages of infection?
questions.explanation: Fimbriae attach bacteria to host tissue, and a capsule aids adherence and biofilm formation — both work toward staying attached to a surface.

questions.prompt: Which statement comparing Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and Acid-Fast cell walls is FALSE?

options.text: Gram-positive walls lack an outer membrane.
Gram-negative walls contain LPS in an outer membrane.
Acid-Fast walls are structurally closest to Gram-negative, since both lack extra peptidoglycan.

questions.explanation: False — Acid-Fast walls are structurally closer to Gram-POSITIVE (no outer membrane, peptidoglycan present), not Gram-negative.

questions.prompt: An antibiotic hydrolyzes peptidoglycan, similar to lysozyme. Explain why this drug would likely be far less effective against Mycobacterium tuberculosis than against Streptococcus pyogenes, even though both technically have a peptidoglycan layer.
questions.explanation: M. tuberculosis's peptidoglycan is coated with waxy mycolic acid, which shields it from enzymes/drugs that would otherwise break it down. S. pyogenes (Gram-positive, no mycolic acid) has more exposed, accessible peptidoglycan for the drug to act on.

questions.prompt: Penicillin has little effect on cells lacking a cell wall (like Mycoplasma), and lysozyme in tears/saliva also fails against Mycoplasma for a similar underlying reason. What is that shared reason?

options.text: Both target peptidoglycan, which Mycoplasma does not have

questions.explanation: Penicillin and lysozyme both act on peptidoglycan; an organism with no cell wall has nothing for either one to target.

questions.prompt: A capsule made of carbohydrate allows Streptococcus mutans to form a biofilm on teeth. Which other structure discussed in this module also contributes to bacterial adherence, though it is made of protein rather than carbohydrate?
questions.explanation: Fimbriae are protein filaments used for adherence, working toward the same general goal (attachment) as the carbohydrate capsule, via a different structure.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of shape/arrangement to disease-causing organism is CORRECT, based on this module's microbe spotlights?

options.text: Cluster of cocci — Streptococcus pyogenes — Strep throat

questions.explanation: Treponema pallidum is a spirochete that causes syphilis. (S. aureus forms clusters, not diplococci; M. tuberculosis is Acid-Fast, not vibrio-shaped; S. pyogenes forms chains, not clusters.)

questions.prompt: Which statement about flagella, fimbriae, and pili is FALSE?

options.text: All three are made of protein.
Fimbriae are used for genetic material exchange.
The conjugation (sex) pilus is used to exchange genetic material.
Fimbriae are tipped with an adhesin protein for attachment.

questions.explanation: False — fimbriae are used for adherence/attachment, not genetic exchange; that role belongs to the conjugation pilus.

questions.prompt: A bacterium is Gram-negative, has an outer membrane with LPS, and forms a capsule. Explain two separate reasons this organism might be especially difficult for the immune system or antibiotics to deal with.
questions.explanation: The outer membrane (with LPS) can block many antibiotics from reaching the peptidoglycan or cell interior. The capsule impedes phagocytosis by immune cells and allows adherence/biofilm formation — both features make the organism harder to clear.

questions.prompt: If a lab technician wants to confirm whether an unknown bacterium relies on mycolic acid in its cell wall, rather than simply being Gram-positive, which test should they use instead of the standard Gram stain?
questions.explanation: The Acid-Fast stain specifically detects mycolic acid's resistance to standard staining, distinguishing it from ordinary Gram-positive organisms.

questions.prompt: Why is the conjugation (sex) pilus considered clinically significant beyond simply enabling genetic exchange?

options.text: It can spread antibiotic-resistance genes carried on plasmids between bacteria
It produces ATP for the cell
It forms the bacterial cell wall

questions.explanation: By transferring plasmids between cells, the conjugation pilus can spread antibiotic resistance genes through a bacterial population.

questions.prompt: Which structure would a vaccine targeting bacterial ADHERENCE most likely need to block, based on structures discussed in this module?
questions.explanation: Fimbriae and capsules are the structures directly responsible for adherence to host tissue or surfaces.

questions.prompt: A Gram stain shows an unknown sample as pink, and the same cells later resist an Acid-Fast stain (don't retain the red dye). What can be concluded?

options.text: The cells are Gram-negative and not Acid-Fast — likely a typical Gram-negative bacterium rather than a mycolic-acid-containing organism
The cells are definitely Mycobacterium tuberculosis
The cells have no cell wall at all

questions.explanation: Pink = Gram-negative; failing to retain the Acid-Fast stain means it lacks mycolic acid, consistent with an ordinary Gram-negative organism, not an Acid-Fast one.

questions.prompt: Explain why a genus like Mycoplasma, which has no cell wall, still requires some structural support to maintain its integrity — referencing what this module says it relies on instead.
questions.explanation: Mycoplasma uses sterols in its cell membrane for stability in place of a rigid peptidoglycan wall, which is also why it is pleiomorphic (variable in shape).
